title: Northstar: a small customer's migration
disclosure: Synthetic interview — fictional company and speaker

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How did your small Northstar deployment migrate?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Our small deployment moved in six weeks because we used only standard connectors.

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: We had twelve users and did not maintain custom integrations. This was one migration, not a representative survey.

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: I cannot estimate how an enterprise deployment would compare.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Can you describe a specific preparation task and how it was handed off?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: One key preparation task was auditing user access rights before migration. I reviewed permissions for each of the twelve users to ensure they matched the new system’s requirements. This audit was then handed off to our IT support team, who confirmed the settings in the target environment. An uncertainty arose because some legacy permissions were not clearly documented, so we had to infer access levels from user activity logs. This workaround introduced some risk, but the IT team cross-checked with users directly to minimize errors. However, I could not fully verify if all inferred permissions were perfect.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How did you implement recordkeeping during migration, and what was a workaround?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: We implemented recordkeeping by maintaining a shared spreadsheet tracking each migration step and user status. Since our standard connectors didn’t log all transfer details automatically, we manually noted any exceptions or errors encountered. A practical workaround was to assign one team member to update the spreadsheet in real time during migration sessions. However, we could not observe all background processes of the connectors, so some automated actions remained opaque to us. This meant our records were comprehensive but not exhaustive, relying on manual observation to fill gaps.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How might a colleague misunderstand your local migration process and its limits?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: A colleague unfamiliar with our process might assume that all migration steps were fully automated and logged by the connectors. I explained that while standard connectors handled most data transfer, manual steps and checks were necessary due to undocumented legacy permissions and incomplete logs. I clarified that our recordkeeping was partly manual and that some background processes were not visible to us. This helped set realistic expectations about the migration’s transparency and the need for human oversight, preventing misunderstandings about the completeness of automated tracking.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How did you arrange shared workspaces and label storage during migration?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: We arranged shared workspaces by designating a single digital folder for all migration documents, which was accessible to the whole team. For physical storage, we labeled boxes containing hardware and printed materials with simple colored stickers. Sometimes the stickers faded or were misplaced, so we used a secondary labeling system with handwritten notes on the boxes. This workaround helped keep materials organized despite occasional label wear. Although this process was unrelated to migration software, it was important for coordinating physical resources and ensuring no materials were lost during the move.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How did you manage meeting agendas and shift notes during the migration?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Meeting agendas were shared via email before each session, but sometimes last-minute changes caused confusion. To manage this, we kept a shared online document where shift notes and agenda updates were posted in real time. When someone missed a meeting, they could catch up by reading these notes. However, not everyone updated the document consistently, so we occasionally had to remind team members to add their notes. This workaround was not related to migration software but helped maintain communication flow during the project.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Can you give an example of passing a task to a colleague while noting your observation limits?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: I once passed the responsibility for validating user permissions post-migration to a colleague in IT support. I informed them that while I had reviewed permissions based on available documentation and logs, some legacy settings were inferred and not fully verifiable. I emphasized that they should double-check with users directly to confirm access rights. This handoff included sharing my notes on uncertainties and the manual steps taken. By communicating these limits, I ensured the colleague understood the potential gaps in my observations and could plan additional verification accordingly.
